summaries.example: Imagine two friends meeting at a park without texting first. They might both choose the playground because it is the easiest place to notice. If they keep meeting there, that choice can become a shared habit. It is useful because each friend expects the other to follow it, but another meeting place could have worked too.
summaries.summary: A convention is a shared pattern that people follow because they expect others to follow it. For example, drivers in a country may all use the right side of the road. This is different from a regular event such as breathing, because people’s choices and expectations help maintain the pattern. Conventions do not always begin with a meeting, promise, or written agreement. They can grow when people discover that following the same plan helps everyone. Philosophers ask how conventions begin, why people obey them, and whether they are habits, norms, rules, or something else. They also ask whether important things such as money and language depend on convention. Some philosophers think language gets meaning from shared ways of using words. Others think language depends more on people’s minds and abilities than on social agreement. The central lesson is that many parts of social life are made possible by shared expectations, but philosophers disagree about exactly how this happens.
key_ideas: Conventions are shared patterns that people can follow because they expect others to follow them too.
Not every common behavior is a convention. Eating and sleeping are regular actions, but they are not usually chosen as shared rules.
A convention can grow without anyone making a formal agreement.
Different conventions may serve the same purpose, so a group must sometimes settle on one.
Some philosophers use convention to explain money, property, government, or language, while others think convention is not enough.
Philosophers disagree about whether conventions are mainly habits, useful choices, rules, or shared commitments.
summaries.why_it_matters: Conventions help people live and act together. They can make traffic safer, help money work as a way to trade, and give words shared meanings. Studying conventions also teaches us to ask whether a rule is natural, necessary, or simply one choice among several workable choices.

important_terms.definition: A shared way of doing something that a group follows, even though another way might have worked.
A pattern that happens often. A regular pattern is not always a convention: breathing is regular, but it is not something people choose together.
A reason people can act together successfully, such as choosing the same meeting place or driving on the same side of the road.
The idea that something depends partly on human choices or shared practices rather than only on nature.

questions_to_think_about: What is a convention in your classroom or family?
How is a traffic rule different from everyone simply getting sleepy at night?
Could two groups use different conventions for the same activity?
Does a convention need a written rule?
Why might people keep following an old convention?

summaries.example: Consider two drivers approaching a narrow intersection where there is no traffic signal. If both expect vehicles to keep to the right, each has a reason to do so, provided the other drivers follow the same practice. Keeping right is not merely a frequently observed behavior: it is a self-reinforcing solution to a recurring coordination problem. Yet the practice is also somewhat arbitrary, since keeping left could have served the same general purpose if everyone had adopted it.
summaries.summary: Philosophical work on convention begins by distinguishing shared conventions from mere regularities. A regularity such as sleeping is widespread but not conventional, whereas driving on one side of the road depends on coordinated expectations and could have been organized differently. Hume describes conventions as arrangements that serve mutual interests and arise without explicit agreement. Lewis gives this idea a formal game-theoretic form: a convention is a recurring, self-reinforcing solution to a coordination problem, supported by expectations that others will conform. Because several solutions may be available, conventions are often arbitrary in the sense that another arrangement could have worked. Critics argue that this model may be too strict about actual conformity and may overlook norms, sanctions, precedent, unequal interests, and conventions that do not solve coordination problems. Other accounts emphasize collective commitment or the historical weight of established practice. A further issue is equilibrium selection: even when several stable arrangements exist, why does a group settle on one? Philosophers appeal to salience, learning, evolutionary or dynamical processes, and psychological mechanisms, but no single explanation is accepted. Conventionalism applies the idea more broadly, claiming that some facts or standards depend on conventions. The source also discusses attempts to explain linguistic meaning through conventions of truthfulness and trust. Objections include the productivity of language, the possibility that language does not fundamentally depend on social convention, and the worry that thought and language may explain one another rather than having a simple one-way order.
key_ideas: Hume explains convention through mutual benefit, expectations, and coordinated action without requiring explicit promises.
Lewis develops a game-theoretic account: conventions are self-perpetuating solutions to recurring coordination problems and are often arbitrary among alternatives.
Lewis’s analysis has been criticized for requiring too much conformity, common knowledge, rational self-understanding, and coordination.
Some alternatives treat conventions as jointly accepted principles, practices serving collective ends, or patterns sustained mainly by precedent and imitation.
Equilibrium selection asks why one possible convention becomes established. Salience, learning, population dynamics, and experiment have all been proposed as parts of the answer.
Conventionalist theories extend beyond social practices. They claim that areas such as meaning, geometry, logic, or morality may depend partly on convention, but these claims face serious objections.
summaries.why_it_matters: Conventions connect individual choices with social order. They help explain how people coordinate without a central authority and how practices such as money or language can function across a group. The topic also tests a larger philosophical distinction: which features of the world are natural or mind-independent, and which depend on human practices, expectations, or choices? That distinction affects debates about norms, meaning, science, mathematics, and social institutions.

important_terms.definition: A regular pattern in a group that is maintained partly because participants expect others to follow it and have reason to conform when others do.
A situation with several possible ways for people to act together successfully, where incompatible choices can prevent the shared benefit.
A stable strategic arrangement in which no participant can gain by changing their action alone, given the actions of others.
The view that some phenomenon is determined by convention, often because alternative conventions could have served a similar purpose.
A situation in which everyone knows something, everyone knows that everyone knows it, and so on through indefinitely many levels.
A choice that stands out among alternatives and therefore may help people converge on one shared practice.
The claim that a convention has a rule-like or should-like force, not merely that people usually behave in a certain way.
The philosophical issue of whether meanings arise from shared linguistic practices or instead from individual cognitive capacities and interpretation.

questions_to_think_about: Must a convention solve a coordination problem, or can rules that constitute a practice—such as the rules of a game—also count?
Can a practice be a convention if people follow it without recognizing alternatives?
Does a convention’s normativity reduce to self-interest, or does it involve a distinct kind of obligation?
Why might a language-based theory struggle to explain our ability to understand indefinitely many new sentences?
When selecting among equilibria, can rational reflection alone choose one, or is shared salience or historical learning required?

summaries.example: Suppose students at a school entrance must choose which side of a crowded hallway to use. If nearly everyone walks on the right, a new student has a reason to do the same: otherwise people may bump into one another. Walking on the right is not the only possible solution; everyone could have walked on the left. The practice works because students expect one another to follow it.
summaries.summary: A convention is a shared way of acting that continues because people expect others to use it and have some reason to do so when others comply. This makes conventions different from mere regularities: people breathe and sleep regularly, but these activities are not usually coordinated choices. A hallway practice or traffic system, by contrast, can solve a recurring problem in which people must fit their actions together. Hume explains conventions through mutual advantage and shared expectations, while Lewis gives a more formal account using game theory. On Lewis’s view, a convention is a stable solution to a coordination problem, and it is often arbitrary because a different solution could have worked. Critics question whether people must nearly always follow a convention, whether participants must understand its alternatives, and whether conventions are essentially normative. Some philosophers also argue that conventions need not solve coordination problems at all; they may help create a practice or be sustained by precedent. Conventionalism is the broader doctrine that some things are determined by convention. It has been applied to social institutions and to debates about geometry, logic, mathematics, morality, and language. Language raises a special challenge: although words are not naturally tied to what they mean, it is disputed whether social convention explains the full structure and productivity of language.
key_ideas: Conventions are different from natural or unavoidable regularities because they depend on shared human practices.
They can develop without a written contract or an official meeting; people may gradually settle into a pattern.
Hume emphasizes common interest and mutual expectations, while Lewis analyzes convention using game theory.
A convention may be arbitrary because another incompatible arrangement could have worked as well.
Philosophers debate whether every convention solves a coordination problem and whether convention includes a special kind of norm or obligation.
Conventionalism says that some topics, including money, property, geometry, or language, may depend on human conventions, but philosophers disagree about how far this goes.
summaries.why_it_matters: Conventions show how large-scale cooperation can arise from ordinary people’s expectations and choices. They help us understand why money can be accepted, why traffic systems work, and why words can communicate. Studying them also helps us examine familiar rules critically: a practice may be useful and deeply established without being the only possible way to organize life.

important_terms.definition: A shared pattern of behavior that helps a group act together and is supported by expectations about what others will do.
A repeated pattern. It becomes a convention only when shared choices and expectations help explain why it continues.
A situation in which people need to match or fit their actions to gain a benefit, even though more than one matching plan may be possible.
A stable choice pattern where no person would do better by changing alone while everyone else keeps their choices.
The idea that something comes from a convention and might have been arranged differently without changing its purpose.
A feature that makes one option seem especially noticeable or natural compared with other options.
The idea that a convention can tell people how they should act, not merely describe what they usually do.

questions_to_think_about: What shared practice at school depends on everyone expecting others to follow it?
Could a convention exist even if people do not know that another convention was possible?
Is following a convention always in your self-interest?
How could an old habit become a rule that people think others ought to obey?
Why might philosophers disagree about whether language is fundamentally conventional?
